evidence.label: Endpoint convergence for the planar Schrodinger equation
Endpoint pointwise convergence for the Schrodinger equation in higher dimensions

headline: Claimed proofs that Schrödinger waves return to rough data at the exact smoothness threshold, in dimensions n ≥ 2.
scope: The claims cover the free Schrödinger equation on ℝⁿ for n ≥ 2, at the endpoint Sobolev exponent n/(2(n + 1)).
plain: The free Schrödinger equation describes a quantum particle moving with no forces. Carleson asked how smooth the starting data must be for the solution to return to it. The return should hold at almost every point as time goes to zero. Earlier work proved convergence for every smoothness strictly above n/(2(n + 1)), and showed nothing below works. These two papers claim convergence exactly at that threshold, in the plane and in every dimension from three up.
doesNot: This does not prove the stronger endpoint L³ maximal estimate in the plane, and it does not cover one dimension.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Lennart Carleson, who posed the pointwise convergence problem
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle the equality case of Carleson's problem, after the strict range was proved in 2017 and 2019.

explanation:
Start with a smooth bump on the plane, f(x) = e^(−|x|²/2). Run the free Schrödinger equation, the basic equation for a quantum particle with no forces. For this bump the solution has a closed form. At the centre its size is 1/√(1 + 4t²). At t = 0.1 that is 1/√1.04, about 0.981. As t shrinks to 0, it returns to 1, the starting value.

Rough starting data is harder. A piece of the wave with frequency N moves at speed 2N. With N = 100, it covers one unit of distance by time t = 0.005. So many fast pieces could make the solution swing wildly as t shrinks. Carleson asked how smooth f must be for the solution to return to f at almost every point. Smoothness is measured by the Sobolev space H^s, where frequency N carries a weight of about N^s.

Carleson proved convergence on the line at s = 1/4[1]. Dahlberg and Kenig showed that this threshold is necessary[2]. Sjölin and Vega independently got s > 1/2 in higher dimensions[3]. In the plane, a run of results lowered the bound to 15/32, 2/5 and then 3/8[4,5]. Bourgain's counterexample showed that s ≥ n/(2(n + 1)) is needed when n ≥ 2. It did not rule out equality[6]. In the plane that number is 2/(2 × 3) = 1/3. Du, Guth and Li proved planar convergence for every s > 1/3[7]. Du and Zhang proved the strict range s > n/(2(n + 1)) for n ≥ 3[8].

The planar paper claims convergence at exactly s = 1/3[9]. The second paper claims the endpoint s = n/(2(n + 1)) for every n ≥ 3[10]. For n = 3 that is 3/8, and for n = 4 it is 2/5. Both papers say exactly how the solution is defined for rough data. They first smooth the data with a Gaussian factor and remove it, then let t go to 0[11]. One set of full measure works for every time at once[12]. Full measure means it leaves out only a set of zero volume.

The main step is a maximal estimate at the exact exponent[13]. A maximal estimate bounds the largest size of the solution over all times 0 ≤ t < 1. In the plane, the paper proves it with a weaker, local L¹ form of output. The stronger endpoint L³ maximal estimate is not claimed[14].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for either paper, so no computer proof checker has tested them. Both papers are long and build on the Du–Guth–Li and Du–Zhang methods. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the papers hold. They settle an equality case after the strict range was known. There is no Lean scope note, and no specialist review is published.

At every point except a set of zero area or volume.

The exact threshold value of s, as opposed to every value strictly above it.

claims.sourceQuote: For every fixed integer $n\geq3$ and every complex-valued $f\in H^{s_n}(\R^n)$, there is a full-measure set $E_f$ of Lebesgue points of $f$ and a function $v(x,t)$, $x\in E_f$, $0\leq t<1$, such that $v(x,\cdot)$ is continuous, $v(x,0)=f^*(x)$, and \begin{equation}\label{m:eq-uniform-Gaussian} \lim_{a\downarrow0}\sup_{0<t<1}|U_af(x,t)-v(x,t)|=0 \qquad(x\in E_f). \end{equation}
